# B2B SaaS Support

`customer_support.model.b2b.saas` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2b`

> Multi-tenant software sold to businesses. This vertical inherits almost everything from B2B support — entitlement is contractual, the requester is an admin and not the buyer, complexity is configuration-specific — and only two things are structurally its own. First, multi-tenancy collapses "one ticket" into "an incident" faster than anywhere else in the domain. The same defect reaches every tenant on the same code path simultaneously, so the third similar report inside an hour is not a coincidence to be triaged three times; it is an incident that has not been declared yet, and the deduplication decision is the highest-value judgement in the queue. Second, the resolution locus is our own codebase. We can unilaterally ship the fix, which means "workaround now, fix next release" is a genuine two-step plan rather than a euphemism for abandonment — and it also means an unfixed defect is a choice we made, which customers correctly read as one. The error an operator carries in from hardware_iot or logistics is assuming resolution needs a third party and pacing the customer accordingly. The error carried in from B2C is treating a burst of similar tickets as a volume problem to staff around rather than a single fault to find.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | an admin, developer or integration owner inside the customer, usually technical enough to have already read the docs |
| typical_resolution_hours | 20 |
| volume_shape | moderate and business-hours shaped, with sharp post-deploy spikes on our release calendar and on the customer's own upgrade windows |
| staffing_model | tiered L1/L2 with product-area specialists and a standing engineering escalation rota |
| coverage | business hours per region, on-call for severity-1 and for declared incidents |
| automation_level | moderate — docs and macros cover the how-do-I third; the configuration-specific remainder resists deflection and always will |
| notes | typical_resolution_hours is the median across a queue whose tail is very long: a config question closes in an hour, a confirmed defect waits for a release train. Reading the median as the experience is the classic SaaS support reporting error.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `product_area_ref`, `issue_ref`


> Both become mandatory because they are what makes clustering possible. A ticket without a product area cannot join the count that declares an incident, and a ticket without an issue link cannot tell you that forty customers hit the same thing — which is exactly the question the roadmap needs support to answer.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`


> Blast radius here is a tenant list, not an estimate. A shared code path makes the affected population computable rather than guessed, and an incident record that leaves it blank in SaaS is under-using information we already have.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `verified_against_version`


> Article accuracy has a version, not a date. An article verified last month against a release that shipped since is stale in a way a timestamp cannot express, and stale self-service is worse than absent self-service because it burns the customer's trust before they reach a human.
